title: School's PERMAnent Value
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Recapping a rough-draft talk he gave the day before, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that 'success' has become too vague and too overloaded a word to usefully guide schooling, and that the resulting confusion is a real source of frustration for both students and adults in schools. He proposes replacing fuzzy success-talk with a clearer purpose statement: school exists to promote long-term flourishing by teaching students toward mastery of disciplines, not to prepare them narrowly for a job or a test score. He grounds 'long-term flourishing' in Martin Seligman's PERMA framework (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, achievement) from Flourish, arguing it gives the otherwise-fuzzy idea rigor. Stuart connects this directly to concerns about AI, arguing that techno-optimist visions of AI doing the learning for students underestimate how much doing hard intellectual work is itself part of what it takes for a person to flourish. He closes by pointing to a specific timestamp in the full talk where he shares Caleb Nothwehr's classroom story as a real-world illustration of the argument.
points: Stuart's core claim is that 'success' is no longer a useful organizing word for schooling because it means simultaneously too much and too little, and that this ambiguity itself generates frustration and wasted effort in schools.

He replaces vague success-talk with a specific purpose statement — school exists to promote long-term flourishing via mastery of disciplines — reframing subjects like math and history as vehicles for flourishing rather than narrow job prep.

Martin Seligman's PERMA framework (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, achievement) is used to give 'long-term flourishing' empirical and conceptual rigor rather than leaving it as an inspirational platitude.

Techno-optimist visions of AI replacing the work of learning are challenged directly: doing hard things is framed as part of what it takes to flourish as a human, not an inefficiency to be automated away.
Even individual teachers adopting a clearer definition of success, absent systemic change, is presented as capable of producing meaningful improvement in an otherwise 'untenable situation.'
quotes: Success isn't a useful word anymore because it means both too much and too little.
First up, this is what schools are for: the promotion of long-term flourishing via teaching students toward mastery of disciplines.
Woe to those who see the Value of a thing only through the impoverished lens of "when will I ever need this?

But the pursuit of long-term flourishing isn't a technicolor montage set to a rock ballad. In a school setting, the pursuit of long-term flourishing is the day-in, day-out work of reading, writing, speaking, building knowledge, arguing, asking questions, and practicing.

Folks who envision a techno-optimist future where AI does it all for us? They underestimate the degree to which doing hard things (e.g., learning math, practicing science, etc.) is part of what it takes to flourish as a human being.
